extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of moral philosophy; educated general readers interested in human nature, will, and liberty
extracted.subtask_description: A close-prose philosophical treatment of what determines the human will, the role of desire and uneasiness, the nature of liberty, and why people pursue different (sometimes bad) courses. The text offers prescriptive and explanatory claims about how to govern desires and exercise freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: But any great Uneasiness is never neglected
rubrics_metrics.description: The will is determined by uneasiness: any great and prevailing uneasiness, once it lays hold on the will, keeps it steady and intent and does not let it go while it lasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: vehement bodily pain, impetuous love, impatient desire of revenge — these keep the will steady and occupy thoughts and actions uninterruptedly; use introspection ('I desire every one to observe in himself') to verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire accompanies all Uneasiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneasiness (including aversion, fear, anger, envy, shame, etc.) always carries desire with it; desire is the chief and most sensible accompaniment of passions and the proximate mover of voluntary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The will seldom issues any voluntary action without some desire; even joy contains desire (to continue) and fear (to lose). Beware conflating will and desire — but acknowledge they are habitually joined.

rubrics_metrics.name: The most pressing Uneasiness naturally determines the Will
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple uneasinesses and desires compete, ordinarily the one most pressing (and judged capable of being then removed) determines the next voluntary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The will cannot be moved toward what is judged unattainable; therefore urgent, addressable discomforts spur action. The will's proper object is some action within our power; prioritize actions that most immediately relieve present uneasiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: All desire Happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness (and the absence of misery) is the ultimate object of desire; pleasures are 'good' and pains 'evil' and we compare goods and evils to judge what to desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good and evil often lie in comparison; smaller pains as well as greater pleasures count as goods/evils insofar as they affect happiness. This grounds why desire ultimately seeks happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only goods considered part of one's happiness are desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every good moves a particular person's desire — only that portion of good which is considered a necessary part of HIS happiness will excite his desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: one man may relish sensual pleasures, another knowledge; each recognizes the other's pleasure but does not desire it because it is not part of his own happiness. The will is indifferent to goods not judged essential to one's happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absent greatest Good often fails to move the Will
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest absent good (even eternal bliss) does not always raise desire proportionally because absent goods do not necessarily form part of present happiness, whereas present uneasiness does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since nothing future is yet in possession, present moderate pleasures may suffice to content; people often neglect even the possibility of greater future good because present satisfactions and recurring uneasinesses dominate attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present necessities and accumulated desires block remote goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary necessities (hunger, thirst, heat, labour, acquired habits) produce a succession of uneasinesses that frequently prevent remoter absent goods from determining the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because life is rarely free from these solicitations, absent goods must be repeatedly contemplated and given relish to raise desire and compete with present uneasiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due Consideration raises Desire
rubrics_metrics.description: By due consideration and examining an absent good, one can raise desire proportional to its value so it may come to determine the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated contemplation brings absent good nearer to the mind and produces a relish; hence exercising reflection is a practical means to align desires with true value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to suspend a desire is the source of Liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to suspend the execution and satisfaction of desires—so as to examine and weigh them before acting—is the hinge of liberty and the source of what is (improperly) called free-will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspension allows one to 'look before' and judge the good or evil of actions and thus to act according to the last result of fair examination; failure to suspend causes mistakes and faults in conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being determined by our own Judgment is no Restraint to Liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: To have one's will determined by the last judgment of one's own understanding is not a diminution of freedom; true freedom consists in acting according to sound judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: preferring to stay in an open prison because of weather is still freedom; the certainer the determination by judgment, the greater the perfection. Freedom is compatible with being determined by what one judges best.

rubrics_metrics.name: The freest agents are determined by the best good
rubrics_metrics.description: Superior beings who enjoy perfect happiness are more steadily determined by choice of good yet are not less free; even God cannot choose what is not good — being determined by good does not negate freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to counter the notion that indifference or indeterminacy is the mark of freedom; freedom improves as determination by right judgment increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursuit of true Happiness undergirds Liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of pursuing true happiness establishes the foundation of liberty: the more one is committed to that greatest good, the more one is obliged to suspend particular satisfactions until judged consistent with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This necessity motivates deliberation and wariness, making suspension and examination duties for agents seeking true felicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government of Passions is the proper improvement of Liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraint, moderation, and governance of passions so that the understanding can examine are the correct exercise and improvement of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extreme disturbances (rack, violent passions) excuse loss of deliberative power; otherwise one ought to train oneself to govern passions by resolution and practice so that judgment remains unbiassed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of pursuits does not prove lack of pursuit of happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: That men choose different and sometimes contrary courses does not show they do not pursue happiness; it shows that individuals place happiness in different things (different 'relishes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to palate: like differing tastes for food, men prefer different goods; philosophers disputing summum bonum erred in assuming a single object of happiness for all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong judgments (especially about future goods) explain choosing misery
rubrics_metrics.description: People choose what makes them miserable not willingly but by wrong judgment — especially by mismeasuring present versus future pleasures/pains or by judging that certain things are not necessary parts of their happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes of wrong judgment include bodily pain forcing choices, misjudging what constitutes necessary happiness, and temporal bias that overvalues present goods; remedy is improved judgment via reflection and correct comparison of consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present vs Future bias: men err in comparing temporal goods
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing present pleasure/pain with future ones, people often mismeasure due to proximity bias: nearer objects are thought greater than larger but more remote ones, causing preference for immediate small goods over larger future ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: preferring little in hand to much to come; drinking now despite later sickness. The correct judgment recognizes the future will become present and vindicate higher value.
